title: The empty det: there is, it says, it was her who
title_target: Det ligger en tvättstuga precis under mitt rum.
goal: Use *det* as an empty subject — with *finns*, with the position verbs *står, ligger, sitter, hänger*, with weather and smells — and put the spotlight on one word with a cleft sentence.
bekal: you can say where things are with *det ligger / står / sitter / hänger* + an indefinite noun
you can stress one element with *Det var Karin som…* and ask *Vem var det som…?*
you can choose between *den*, *det* and *de* when you refer back to something
wave: Go back to Unit 3: take five sentences with a fronted object or adverbial (*Den filmen har jag sett*) and say each one again as a cleft (*Det är den filmen som jag har sett*) — notice that both versions shine the spotlight on the same word.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Rummet i Majorna
dialogs.intro: Oskar drops by the room Dian rents in Majorna, an old working-class district by the harbor. The chest of drawers from the flea market is in place, and now he looks around with a critical eye.

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Vad mysigt! Men det luktar lite fukt här, eller?
lines.id: How cozy! But it smells a bit damp in here, doesn't it?
lines.literal: what cozy! but it smells a-little damp here, or?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Det är källaren. Det ligger en tvättstuga precis under mitt rum.
lines.id: That's the basement. There's a laundry room right under my room.
lines.literal: it is basement-the. it lies a laundry-room exactly under my room.

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Och vad är det som sitter på dörren där? En lapp?
lines.id: And what's that on the door there? A note?
lines.literal: and what is it that sits on door-the there? a note?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Ja, det står att man måste boka tvättid i förväg. Det sitter en likadan i hallen.
lines.id: Yes, it says you have to book a laundry slot in advance. There's an identical one in the hall.
lines.literal: yes, it stands that one must book wash-time in advance. it sits a same-kind in hall-the.

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Typiskt svenskt. Finns det en mikro också?
lines.id: Typically Swedish. Is there a microwave as well?
lines.literal: typically Swedish. exists it a micro also?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Nej, men det finns ett litet kök som jag delar med tjejen i rummet bredvid.
lines.id: No, but there's a small kitchen that I share with the girl in the room next door.
lines.literal: no, but it exists a little kitchen that I share with girl-the in room-the beside.

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Och den här stora växten? Den ser nästan död ut.
lines.id: And this big plant? It looks almost dead.
lines.literal: and this here big plant-the? it looks almost dead out.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Den är inte min, det är Hannas, hon som jag hyr av. Hon bad mig att vattna den.
lines.id: It's not mine, it's Hanna's — she's the one I rent from. She asked me to water it.
lines.literal: it is not mine, it is Hanna's, she who I rent from. she asked me to water it.

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Då är det nog du som har glömt det.
lines.id: Then I guess you're the one who forgot.
lines.literal: then is it probably you who has forgotten it.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Tyst! Det har regnat i tre veckor, så jag trodde att den fick vatten ändå.
lines.id: Quiet! It's been raining for three weeks, so I thought it was getting water anyway.
lines.literal: quiet! it has rained in three weeks, so I thought that it got water anyway.

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Den står inomhus, Dian. Det är inte så det fungerar.
lines.id: It's indoors, Dian. That's not how it works.
lines.literal: it stands indoors, Dian. it is not so it works.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Okej, okej. Det finns en kanna i köket. Jag fixar det.
lines.id: Okay, okay. There's a watering can in the kitchen. I'll take care of it.
lines.literal: okay, okay. it exists a can in kitchen-the. I fix it.

notes: **Det luktar lite fukt** — Swedish needs a subject in every main clause, so when nobody is doing anything it brings in an empty *det*: *det regnar*, *det snöar*, *det blåser* (it's windy), *det luktar* (it smells), *det är kallt*. English does exactly the same with "it" — the difference comes in the next note.

**Det ligger en tvättstuga…** — where English says "there is", Swedish often prefers a **position verb**: things that lie flat or are placed somewhere *ligger*, upright things *står*, things fixed to something *sitter*, hanging things *hänger*. Buildings and places always *ligger*: *Det ligger ett kafé på hörnet.* *Det finns* is the neutral choice when position doesn't matter.

**det står att…** — for written text, *stå* means "to say": *Vad står det på lappen?* (What does the note say?), *Det står i tidningen* (It's in the paper). Never use *säga* for a text — *lappen säger* sounds like the note can talk.

**tvättid** (**TVET-teed**) — *tvätt* + *tid*. Swedish traditionally never writes three identical consonants in a row, so *tvätt-tid* became *tvättid*. The *tvättstuga* (shared laundry room) with its booking system is a Swedish institution — and a famous source of neighbor drama when someone takes your slot.

**Den är inte min, det är Hannas** — two kinds of "it" side by side. *Den* points back to *växten* (an en-word) and describes it. *Det är…* simply identifies or presents something, and it stays *det* whatever the gender or number: *Det är min växt*, *Det är mina böcker*.

**Då är det nog du som har glömt det** — a cleft sentence, which you'll meet properly in the next dialogue. Notice the last *det*: it doesn't point to a noun, but to the whole action (forgetting to water). Swedish uses *det* for actions and situations where English often has nothing at all: *Jag fixar det* (I'll take care of it), *Jag vet det* (I know).

grammars.title: Det finns — and its four cousins
body: These sentences all follow the same pattern: empty **det** + verb + the real (logical) subject, which comes later and is almost always **indefinite**.

head: Verb
Used for
Example
rows: things lying flat; buildings, places, cities
**Det står** en cykel på gården. **Det står** i mejlet.
things fixed to something; people sitting

after: With a **definite** subject, drop the empty *det* and use ordinary word order: *Tvättstugan ligger i källaren* — not *Det ligger tvättstugan i källaren*. English works the same way: "There's a laundry room downstairs", but "The laundry room is downstairs".

In questions and after a fronted element, *det* swaps places with the verb (V2): ***Finns det*** *en mikro?* — *I hallen **sitter det** en lapp.* In a subordinate clause, BIFF applies as usual: *…eftersom det **inte finns** någon mikro.*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Vem var det som bokade rummet?
dialogs.intro: Tuesday, ten o'clock. Karin, Mattias and Dian arrive at the big meeting room for their project meeting — and find it already full.

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Det sitter folk i det stora mötesrummet. Var det inte vi som hade bokat det?
lines.id: There are people sitting in the big meeting room. Wasn't it us who'd booked it?
lines.literal: it sits people in the big meeting-room-the. was it not we who had booked it?

lines.speaker: Mattias:
lines.text: Jo, det var Dian som bokade det i måndags.
lines.id: Yes, it was Dian who booked it on Monday.
lines.literal: yes, it was Dian who booked it in Monday.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Det stämmer. Det står i kalendern: tisdag klockan tio, projektgruppen.
lines.id: That's right. It says so in the calendar: Tuesday at ten, project group.
lines.literal: it tallies. it stands in calendar-the: Tuesday clock-the ten, project-group-the.

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Då är det någon annan som har gjort fel. Vilka är det som sitter där?
lines.id: Then it's someone else who's made a mistake. Who's in there?
lines.literal: then is it someone other who has done wrong. who are it that sit there?

lines.speaker: Mattias:
lines.text: Det är ekonomiavdelningen. Det är alltid de som tar rummet utan att boka.
lines.id: It's the finance department. They're always the ones who take the room without booking.
lines.literal: it is economy-department-the. it is always they who take room-the without to book.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Ska jag gå in och säga något?
lines.id: Should I go in and say something?
lines.literal: shall I go in and say something?

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Nej, det är inte värt det. Finns det något annat rum ledigt?
lines.id: No, it's not worth it. Is there another room free?
lines.literal: no, it is not worth it. exists it some other room free?

lines.speaker: Mattias:
lines.text: Det finns ett litet rum på tredje våningen, men det är ganska kallt där.
lines.id: There's a small room on the third floor, but it's pretty cold in there.
lines.literal: it exists a little room on third floor-the, but it is rather cold there.

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Det gör inget. Det viktiga är att vi kommer i gång.
lines.id: That doesn't matter. The important thing is that we get started.
lines.literal: it does nothing. the important is that we come in going.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Jag tar med kaffe. Det blir lättare att tänka då.
lines.id: I'll bring coffee. It'll be easier to think then.
lines.literal: I take with coffee. it becomes easier to think then.

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Det var det bästa förslaget jag har hört i dag.
lines.id: That's the best suggestion I've heard all day.
lines.literal: it was the best suggestion-the I have heard today.

notes: **Det sitter folk…** — *det sitter* also works for people: *Det sitter någon i mitt rum* (Someone's sitting in my room), *Det står en man utanför* (There's a man standing outside). It paints the picture more precisely than *det finns*, which sounds odd with people in a room.

**Det var Dian som bokade det** — a **cleft sentence**: *det är/var* + the element you want to stress + *som* + the rest. English does the same ("It was Dian who…"), but Swedes use clefts far more often, especially in questions: *Vem var det som bokade?* sounds more natural than plain *Vem bokade?*

**Det stämmer** (**deh STEM-mer**) — "That's right", "That's correct". *Stämma* means "to tally, to be correct" (and also "to tune" an instrument). *Stämmer det att du flyttar?* — Is it true that you're moving?

**Det är alltid de som…** — after *det är/var* in a cleft, use the **subject** form of the pronoun: *det är **jag** som*, *det var **hon** som*, *det är **de** (dom) som*. Without the *som*-clause, spoken Swedish often switches to the object form, as English does: *Vem är det? — Det är **mig**!* is common in speech, though *Det är jag* is the standard form.

**Det är inte värt det** (**deh eh IN-teh veht deh**) — "It's not worth it", with two *det*s just like English "it… it". And **Det gör inget** (**deh yör ING-et**), literally "it does nothing", is the everyday "Never mind, no problem".

**Det var det bästa förslaget** — Swedes often use the **past** *det var* to react to something that has just happened, where English uses the present: *Det var gott!* (after a meal: That was / This is delicious), *Det var snällt av dig!* (That's kind of you), *Det var länge sedan!* (Long time no see).

grammars.title: Cleft sentences: putting one word in the spotlight
body: Start from a neutral sentence and pull out the element you want to stress. Everything else goes into a *som*-clause. The tense of *är/var* usually matches the rest of the sentence.

head: Neutral
Cleft (stressing one element)
rows: **Det var i hallen (som)** jag hittade lappen.

after: As always, *som* may be dropped when it is not the subject of its clause (*Det var i hallen jag hittade lappen*), but it must stay when it is (*Det var Dian som bokade*).
The cleft is also the polite way to answer the phone or the door: ***Det är** Dian.* (It's Dian.) And it gives you the very useful question ***Är det** du som är Leila?* — Are you Leila?

blocks.text: When English says "it" or "they", Swedish has to choose. The choice depends on **what** you are pointing at, not on the word "it".

head: Use
When
Example
rows: Var är växten? — **Den** står i hallen.
Var är mötesrummet? — **Det** ligger på tredje våningen.
Var är nycklarna? — **De** ligger på bordet.
you **present or identify** something (any gender, any number)
Vad är det? — **Det** är en kanna. / **Det** är mina nycklar.
you refer to a whole **situation or action**

blocks.text: The typical pair is **presenting** first and **describing** second: *Vad är det där? — **Det** är en växt. **Den** ser nästan död ut.* The first sentence answers "what is it?" and uses *det*; the second describes the plant and uses *den*.

blocks.title: Watch out
items: *Det är kall* is wrong for the weather — the adjective agrees with the empty *det*, so it takes the *-t* form: **Det är kallt.** The same goes for *det är varmt*, *det är fint*, *det är roligt*.
*Det finns* takes an indefinite noun. To say that something specific exists, use *finns* without *det*: **Finns kaffet kvar?** (Is the coffee still there?)
*Det står* = it says (text); *den står* = it stands (an en-word that is upright). Context makes it clear.

blocks.text: In Göteborg, as in Stockholm, it can take years to get a first-hand rental contract, so many newcomers rent a room or an apartment **i andra hand** (second-hand) from someone who holds the contract. Unit 19 looks at the paperwork; here is the everyday vocabulary.

Notes from neighbors are a genre of their own in Sweden. A typical one in a stairwell starts politely and ends sharply: *Till den som tog min tvättid i lördags…* (To whoever took my laundry slot last Saturday…). Now you can read the *den som* in it, too.

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Unit 11
items: Describe your own room or apartment in six sentences, using *det ligger*, *det står*, *det sitter* and *det hänger* at least once each.
Then add one sentence with *det som*: *Det som jag gillar mest är…*
Finish with a cleft: *Det är … som gör rummet mysigt.*
